A_admissions_architecture.primary_application_route: Direct-to-institution in most of Canada; a provincial centralized application platform exists only in Ontario (OUAC), British Columbia (EducationPlannerBC), and Alberta (ApplyAlberta). Quebec has a CEGEP-then-university structure with regional CEGEP admission services (SRAM/SRACQ/SRASL) feeding into a separate, largely direct-to-university stage for the bachelor's degree itself. Other provinces (Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, PEI, Newfoundland & Labrador) have no centralized undergraduate application platform at all — applicants apply directly to each university's own portal.
A_admissions_architecture.centralized_or_decentralized: Genuinely decentralized at the national level. Education is a constitutional responsibility of the provinces/territories in Canada (like the US state pattern), and there is no single pan-Canadian undergraduate application platform equivalent to UCAS. Centralization exists only within specific provinces, and even there it is provincial, not national.
A_admissions_architecture.provincial_variation_note: Ontario: OUAC is the near-universal single application gateway (all Ontario universities use it except Royal Military College of Canada, which processes its own applications). British Columbia: EducationPlannerBC lets applicants apply to multiple BC public post-secondary institutions (including UBC, SFU, UVic, UNBC) through one shared platform, though some like UBC also layer their own supplementary Personal Profile. Alberta: ApplyAlberta links 26 publicly funded Alberta institutions (University of Alberta, University of Calgary, Mount Royal, MacEwan, etc.) for shared application submission and transcript transfer. Quebec: CEGEP admission (the mandatory pre-university step for Quebec residents) is centralized regionally via SRAM (Montreal-area), SRACQ, and SRASL, but admission to the actual bachelor's degree at a Quebec university (e.g., McGill, Université de Montréal) is a separate, university-specific application, evaluated via the province-wide 'R-score' (cote de rendement au collégial) for CEGEP-origin applicants. Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, PEI, Newfoundland: no centralized platform found — direct university-by-university application is the norm.
major_application_platforms: OUAC (Ontario Universities' Application Centre) — Ontario, covers nearly all Ontario universities except Royal Military College of Canada
EducationPlannerBC — British Columbia, covers BC public post-secondary institutions including UBC, SFU, UVic, UNBC
ApplyAlberta — Alberta, covers 26 publicly funded Alberta post-secondary institutions
SRAM / SRACQ / SRASL — Quebec regional CEGEP admission services (pre-university stage only, not the bachelor's degree application itself)
A_admissions_architecture.direct_university_application_possible: Yes, and it is the default/only route outside Ontario, BC, and Alberta. Even within Ontario, RMC requires direct application. Most Quebec, Atlantic, and Prairie universities take direct applications through their own portals.
A_admissions_architecture.application_limit_if_any: OUAC: no fixed cap on the number of Ontario universities a single OUAC application (101 or 105) can be sent to, but choices beyond a base number incur extra per-choice fees (OUAC 105 base fee covers up to 3 program choices, with each additional choice at extra cost, per third-party OUAC guides — official OUAC fee schedule should be confirmed each cycle). ApplyAlberta and EducationPlannerBC likewise allow multiple institution choices within one account, generally with added fees per additional institution/program. Outside these three provinces there is no platform-level limit because each university application is submitted and paid for separately.
A_admissions_architecture.parallel_application_rules: No national restriction on how many Canadian universities a student may apply to in parallel — unlike UCAS's 5-choice cap, Canada allows applying to as many universities as the student is willing to pay separate (or platform) fees for, across as many provinces as desired, with no exclusivity or single-choice mechanism.
A_admissions_architecture.scope: provincial (OUAC=Ontario; EducationPlannerBC=British Columbia; ApplyAlberta=Alberta; SRAM et al.=Quebec CEGEP stage) with a national-level absence-of-system finding for the rest of Canada
sources: https://www.ouac.on.ca/ (OUAC official site, home page and guide sections)

B_qualification_eligibility.recognition_mechanism: No Canada-wide credential-recognition body for undergraduate admission. Each university (or, within Ontario/BC/Alberta, each university operating through the shared platform) independently evaluates foreign secondary credentials against its own published country/qualification-specific minimums. World Education Services (WES) is a NACES-member third-party credential evaluator that some Canadian institutions and, more commonly, immigration (IRCC) and professional licensing bodies rely on or accept, but it is not a universal or mandatory gateway for undergraduate admission — most large Canadian universities (U of T, McGill, UBC, Waterloo, Alberta) publish their own country-specific high-school equivalency tables and evaluate transcripts in-house rather than requiring a WES report for a first-year high-school applicant.
B_qualification_eligibility.baseline_qualification_expectation: A recognized secondary-school leaving credential appropriate to the applicant's country/curriculum (e.g., OSSD for Ontario, DEC for Quebec, a full national high-school diploma for international systems), completed subject prerequisites for the intended program, and (for non-native-English/French speakers) proof of language proficiency. There is no single 'Canadian baseline diploma' — each university states its own minimum for each recognized foreign system.
B_qualification_eligibility.subject_prerequisites_general: Very common at the program level (not just university level): competitive programs such as Engineering, Computer Science, and Business/Commerce typically require specific senior secondary courses (e.g., Calculus, Physics, Chemistry) with stated minimum grades in each, layered on top of the general admission average.
B_qualification_eligibility.equivalency_process: University-specific. Admissions offices maintain internal country-by-country equivalency guides (e.g., University of Toronto's 'International High School Requirements by Country' page) that translate each recognized foreign qualification (MEB diploma, IB, A-Level, French Bac, Abitur, etc.) into an expected minimum grade/average for that institution. There is no centralized Canadian NARIC-equivalent for undergraduate admission purposes (WES exists but serves a broader, largely immigration/professional-licensing role — see below).
B_qualification_eligibility.university_discretion: High. Each university sets its own minimum average, prerequisite courses, and holistic factors (personal profile, supplementary application) per program; there is no national or even reliably provincial standardization of what counts as a 'competitive' foreign applicant, mirroring the very high institutional discretion found in the US system.

credentials_covered.turkiye_meb: Recognized as a foreign secondary credential; individual Canadian universities publish Turkey-specific minimum grade/average expectations on their international country-requirement pages (e.g., University of Toronto's country-by-country list includes Turkey), but exact published thresholds could not be independently verified from a fetched U of T page in this research pass (site blocked automated pagination access) — confidence: medium, university-specific verification needed per target school.
credentials_covered.ib_diploma: Widely and explicitly recognized; most major universities (McGill, Alberta, Waterloo, Toronto, Western) publish IB-specific minimum diploma-point and HL/SL subject requirements and treat IB predicted grades as the basis for a conditional offer, later confirmed against final IB results.
credentials_covered.a_levels: Recognized, generally evaluated similarly to IB — minimum grades in 3 A-Levels (sometimes with specified subjects) form the basis of a conditional offer pending final results; this research pass focused primarily on IB/MEB per the assignment scope; A-Level details are university-specific and were not separately fetched in depth.
credentials_covered.ap_plus_us_diploma: AP exams are used primarily as supplementary evidence of rigor/subject readiness and sometimes for credit/placement, not as a substitute for the US high school diploma itself, mirroring the AP role already documented in the US system.
credentials_covered.french_bac: Recognized as a foreign qualification with university-specific minimum-grade equivalency tables; not independently verified in this research pass.
credentials_covered.german_abitur: Recognized as a foreign qualification with university-specific minimum-grade equivalency tables; not independently verified in this research pass.

turkiye_applicant_view.standard_diploma_sufficient_for_direct_e: Likely yes for many mid-tier and non-restricted programs, but this could not be confirmed with a specific numeric Turkey threshold from an official Canadian university source in this research pass — University of Toronto's country-requirement page structure (paginated, ~8 pages of countries) confirms Turkey is a listed, individually evaluated country but the automated fetch could not retrieve the Turkey-specific row. Treat as an open item requiring direct manual verification per target university (see unresolved_questions).
turkiye_applicant_view.additional_qualifications_commonly_requi: Not confirmed as a formal requirement, but Turkish MEB applicants competing for selective programs (Engineering, Computer Science, Business) will face the same subject-prerequisite and competitive-average pressure as any other international applicant; a strong MEB average alone likely will not be competitive for high-demand programs at top-ranked universities without strong subject grades (Math, Physics, Chemistry as applicable).
turkiye_applicant_view.ap_ib_a_level_impact: Materially strengthens eligibility and competitiveness, consistent with the pattern already found for the US and UK: IB/A-Level curricula from Turkish schools give admissions officers a more internationally standardized, higher-confidence signal than a MEB-only transcript, likely improving both eligibility clarity and competitive positioning, especially for programs with subject-specific HL/SL or A-Level requirements.
turkiye_applicant_view.national_entrance_exam_relevance: LGS (high-school placement exam) and YKS (Turkish national university entrance exam) results are Turkey-domestic instruments tied to Turkish higher-education placement; no evidence found that Canadian universities use or request YKS/LGS scores in undergraduate admission decisions. Not relevant to Canadian admission — consistent with the US/UK pattern already established.
turkiye_applicant_view.foundation_year_common: Not confirmed as common in Canada specifically; no source found describing a widespread Canadian foundation-year pathway for Turkish/MEB applicants analogous to the UK's international foundation year model. Canada appears closer to the US pattern (foundation years are not a standard mainstream pathway) but this is an inference, not a directly sourced finding — flagged for further verification.
turkiye_applicant_view.recognition_centralized_or_university_sp: University-specific. No Canada-wide or even reliably provincial body evaluates Turkish credentials for undergraduate admission; each institution (via its own international admissions office) sets and applies its own Turkey-specific equivalency standard.

academic_evidence_used.transcript_role: Central piece of evidence for all applicant types; Canadian universities evaluate the applicant's own curriculum's grading scale directly rather than universally converting to a single Canadian GPA scale — e.g., McGill evaluates Ontario applicants via a 'Top 6' 4U/4M course average, Quebec CEGEP applicants via the province's R-score, and international applicants via country-specific transcript evaluation. Admission averages/percentages, not a converted 4.0 GPA, are the dominant reporting convention at most Canadian universities (unlike common US practice of GPA conversion).
academic_evidence_used.native_grades_handling: Generally evaluated in the applicant's native scale/system rather than force-converted to a single unified GPA — each university publishes its own country-specific expected minimum in that country's native grading convention (e.g., IB score out of 45, A-Level letter grades, percentage average for provincial Canadian systems). No universal Canadian GPA-recalculation service was found comparable to a formal centralized process; recalculation, where it happens, is done internally and independently by each admissions office.
academic_evidence_used.predicted_grades_role: Used operationally, primarily for IB Diploma (and likely A-Level) applicants who apply before final results are available — universities such as McGill and University of Alberta explicitly state they evaluate applicants 'on predicted IB results' where final results are not yet available, and issue conditional offers on that basis. Not a defining nationwide mechanic the way UK conditional offers are, but a real and commonly used tool for internationally curriculumed applicants (IB/A-Level) specifically, less so for domestic Canadian provincial-curriculum applicants who are typically evaluated on interim/final grades reported directly by their high school (e.g., Ontario's OUAC receives midterm and final 4U/4M grades directly from schools).
academic_evidence_used.final_grades_role: Required to confirm/finalize any conditional offer; e.g. Carleton University requires final IB transcripts by August 15 to confirm admission, and will withdraw an offer if final results fall below the program's required grades.
academic_evidence_used.external_exams_role: IB external exams and A-Level exams are treated as authoritative final results confirming or overturning a conditional offer; MEB does not have an equivalent external final-exam layer beyond the diploma itself (consistent with prior ORYN MEB findings), so MEB-only applicants are evaluated on final transcript grades rather than a predicted-then-confirmed exam process.
academic_evidence_used.course_rigor_signal: Subject-level course selection matters strongly for competitive/prerequisite-bearing programs (e.g., HL vs SL Math for IB, 4U vs 4M level courses in Ontario, A-Level subject choice) — course rigor is evaluated in addition to overall average, not as a substitute for it.
academic_evidence_used.subject_prerequisites: Program-specific prerequisite courses (Calculus, Physics, Chemistry, etc.) are common for Engineering, Computer Science, Business, and health-science-track programs; missing a prerequisite can render an applicant ineligible regardless of overall average.
academic_evidence_used.standardized_tests: Not a defining admission element for most Canadian undergraduate admission (see standardized_tests section below) — grades and prerequisite completion dominate.

predicted_grades.are_used: Yes, specifically and explicitly for IB Diploma applicants (and by strong analogy, A-Level applicants), where final results are not yet available at the time of application.
predicted_grades.where: University-level policy at institutions receiving IB/A-Level applicants before final results are released (McGill, University of Alberta, Carleton, and by pattern most major Canadian universities that admit substantial international IB/A-Level cohorts).
predicted_grades.by_whom: The applicant's IB-authorized school (predicted grades are generated by the IB itself as part of its own assessment process, independent of the destination country, then submitted to the university as part of the application).
predicted_grades.for_what: To make an initial (conditional) admission decision before final IB/A-Level results are published, allowing timely offers ahead of the results release each July.
predicted_grades.conditional_offer_relationship: Predicted grades are the basis for a conditional offer; the offer becomes unconditional (confirmed) only once final results meet or exceed the program's stated minimum grade requirements.
predicted_grades.final_result_requirement: Final official IB (or A-Level) results must be submitted by a stated deadline (e.g., Carleton requires final transcripts by August 15) to confirm admission; universities state they will withdraw the offer, and where possible offer an alternate program, if final results fall short.

conditional_vs_unconditional_admission.concept_exists: Yes, in a form functionally similar to (though less universally central-mechanic-driven than) the UK's conditional-offer system, applied mainly to applicants still completing secondary school.
conditional_vs_unconditional_admission.explanation: Canadian universities commonly issue offers to students still in their final year of secondary school that are 'conditional' on the student maintaining or achieving specified final grades (overall average and/or specific prerequisite course grades). This applies to domestic provincial-curriculum students (e.g., Ontario 4U/4M final grades submitted after the offer) and explicitly to IB/A-Level applicants whose offer is based on predicted grades and confirmed against final results by a stated summer deadline. If final results fall below the required threshold, the university may withdraw the offer or, in some documented cases (Carleton), redirect the applicant to an alternate program for which they do qualify.

subject_prerequisites.pattern: Competitive and technical programs (Engineering, Computer Science, Business/Commerce, health sciences) commonly require specific senior secondary courses completed with a stated minimum grade in each, on top of an overall admission average — a program-level, not university-level or national-level, layer of the system.
illustrative_examples: University of Waterloo Engineering: all Engineering programs require five specific Ontario-equivalent courses — Advanced Functions, Calculus and Vectors, Chemistry, Physics, and English (4U level for Ontario applicants) — each with a minimum final grade of 70%, though competitive admitted averages run into the high-80s to mid-90s depending on the specific program (e.g., Software Engineering low-to-mid 90s).

McGill IB applicants: HL Mathematics (Analysis & Approaches, or Applications & Interpretation) or SL Mathematics AA is accepted as the math prerequisite for most programs, while SL Mathematics: Applications & Interpretation is explicitly NOT accepted as a math prerequisite for programs that require it.

Carleton University IB conditional offers vary by program: e.g., Bachelor of Computer Science requires a minimum final grade of 4 in HL or SL Math; Engineering programs require no final grade lower than 5 in HL or SL Math, Physics, and Chemistry.

standardized_tests.mandatory_optional_status: Generally NOT required for Canadian undergraduate admission, for both domestic and most international applicants — this is a genuine, confirmed system-level difference from the US, where Canadian admission is predominantly grades/transcript-based. Some universities/programs may request or consider SAT/ACT scores as supplementary evidence specifically for international applicants whose local secondary system is less familiar to admissions officers or where transcript comparability is unclear, but this is the exception rather than the rule and is university/program-specific, not a system-wide requirement.
standardized_tests.current_cycle_note: No evidence found of a widespread shift toward requiring SAT/ACT in Canada for the 2026-27/2027-entry cycle; the grades-first pattern appears stable.
standardized_tests.ap_exam_role_in_admissions_vs_credit: Similar to the US pattern already documented: AP exam scores can serve as supplementary evidence of academic rigor/readiness in admission review and are separately used by many Canadian universities for course credit/placement decisions after enrollment, but AP is not itself a substitute for the underlying high school diploma/transcript.

language_requirements.framework: Standard international battery accepted broadly: IELTS, TOEFL, PTE, and Duolingo English Test are commonly accepted across Canadian universities. Canada also has its own purpose-built test, CAEL (Canadian Academic English Language Assessment), which is specifically designed for Canadian academic admission and is accepted by over 180 Canadian universities and colleges; CAEL scores are reported on a 10-90 scale (multiples of 10), with scores above 70 ('Adept' level) generally sufficient for admission to most Canadian universities. CAEL is also recognized by IRCC for the Student Direct Stream (SDS) study-permit fast-track, giving it a dual admission + immigration role distinct from IELTS/TOEFL.
language_requirements.exemption_pattern: Applicants who have completed a substantial portion of secondary education in English (or French, for Quebec French-language institutions) are commonly exempted — e.g., McGill explicitly exempts Quebec CEGEP applicants from English-proficiency proof if they completed (or are completing) a DEC at an English CEGEP, or a DEC at a French CEGEP after the Quebec Secondary V diploma.
language_requirements.where_variation_begins: Minimum accepted scores (IELTS band, TOEFL total, CAEL score, Duolingo score) and which exact tests are accepted vary by university and sometimes by program — this is university-level, not national or provincial, variation.

application_timing.major_deadline_pattern: Most Fall (September)-intake undergraduate deadlines fall between January and March of the entry year. Ontario, via OUAC, has a well-documented 'equal consideration' deadline (commonly January 15) by which Group A (current Ontario high school / OUAC 101) applications should be submitted to receive equal consideration from Ontario universities; the earliest date universities may require a financial commitment/offer response is typically June 1. UBC's international undergraduate deadline for the 2026-27 cycle is reported as January 15, 2027 (tentative), with an earlier October 1–November 15 window offering a first-round-offer option and eligibility for UBC's Presidential Scholars Awards. Quebec/McGill CEGEP-stream deadlines run earlier in some categories (e.g., March 1 application, April 15 supporting documents in a recent cycle, with select programs like Music/Nursing/Social Work opening as early as January 15).
application_timing.provincial_variation: Ontario (via OUAC) enforces a relatively firm, uniform equal-consideration deadline across its member universities. Western Canada and Atlantic Canada institutions tend to offer later windows and more rolling-style flexibility, continuing to accept applications into spring/early summer for Fall intake until programs fill. This rolling, later-deadline pattern relative to UK (single autumn UCAS deadline) and US (rigid ED/EA/RD cycle with October–January deadlines) is a real, sourced system-level characteristic of much of Canada outside Ontario's OUAC-organized deadline structure.

constraints: OUAC (Ontario) allows multiple program/university choices within one account but charges a base fee covering a limited number of choices (reported by third-party OUAC guides as up to 3 for the 105 stream) with additional per-choice fees beyond that — official current fee schedule should be verified directly with OUAC each cycle.

No binding early-decision or Oxbridge-style single-choice exclusivity mechanism exists anywhere in the Canadian system that was found in this research — students may hold and compare multiple simultaneous offers from different Canadian universities (and different provinces) without any binding commitment mechanism analogous to US Early Decision or the UK's Oxbridge one-choice rule.

Some universities (e.g., Western University) group program choices by faculty/direct-entry status, meaning applicants sometimes need not list two programs within the same faculty separately unless one is a distinct direct-entry program with its own OUAC code — a university-specific administrative nuance rather than a general national/provincial constraint.
application_strategy_constraints.explanation: Canada's general lack of a binding early-commitment system, combined with parallel application freedom across universities and provinces, is a real structural contrast to both the US (ED binding commitment) and UK (5-choice UCAS cap, Oxbridge exclusivity). The main real constraints that exist are cost/fee-driven (per-application or per-extra-choice fees) rather than rule-driven exclusivity.

personal_statement_essays.role: Varies significantly by university — not a universal Common-App-style requirement, and not absent the way it often is for many continental European systems either. Most Canadian universities (e.g., University of Toronto's general Arts & Science admission) evaluate primarily on transcript with no required personal essay. UBC is a notable, well-documented exception: it requires a multi-question 'Personal Profile' (up to 8 short essay-style responses, roughly 500-2100 characters each) from effectively all high-school applicants across nearly every program, functioning as a central, heavily weighted holistic component distinct from the norm elsewhere in Canada.
personal_statement_essays.explanation: The pattern is university-specific rather than a defining national or even provincial system feature — a student cannot assume either 'Canada requires an essay' or 'Canada does not require an essay' without checking the specific target university. Competitive/professional-track programs elsewhere (e.g., some Engineering supplementary applications, certain Business programs) may also require a short written component even where the general Arts & Science stream at the same university does not.

recommendation_letters.role: Generally not required for most Canadian undergraduate (bachelor's) admissions — closer to the UK's lighter-emphasis pattern than to the US model where recommendation letters are near-universal. Most institutions rely on transcript-based or transcript-plus-supplementary-application review without a reference-letter component at the undergraduate level.
recommendation_letters.explanation: Where letters do appear, it is typically for specific competitive/professional-track undergraduate programs or scholarship applications rather than as a general admission requirement; this is a program-specific exception layered on a general no-letters baseline, not the reverse.

extracurricular_activities.role: Genuinely variable by institution rather than a stable Canada-wide midpoint between the US and UK patterns. At some universities/programs (e.g., University of Toronto's general Arts & Science admission), extracurriculars are explicitly not considered — admission is transcript-driven only. At others (most notably UBC, via its mandatory Personal Profile), extracurricular depth and leadership are a heavily weighted, near-US-level factor. Competitive/oversubscribed programs elsewhere often use extracurricular/supplementary evidence as a differentiator once the academic threshold is cleared.
extracurricular_activities.nuance: Depth (sustained commitment, leadership, demonstrable outcome) is consistently described as valued over breadth (long list of low-commitment activities) where extracurriculars are considered at all — but whether they are considered at all is the first, university-specific question a counselor must answer before advising a student on how much to invest in this area for a given Canadian target school.

interviews_tests_portfolios.pattern: Not a general undergraduate admission requirement; applies at the programme level for specific creative, performance, and some professional/health-adjacent programs.
interviews_tests_portfolios.when_applicable: Music programs (e.g., University of Toronto Faculty of Music, UBC Music) require an audition and typically an interview as a core admission element. Fine Art/Design programs (e.g., Queen's Fine Art, UBC Bachelor of Design in Architecture) require a portfolio submission, sometimes in place of a general personal-statement-style application. Some professional-adjacent or highly selective programs (e.g., Western's Ivey Advanced Entry Opportunity for Business) use additional structured evaluation components beyond grades. General Arts, Science, and most Engineering/Business direct-entry programs do not require interviews or portfolios.

restricted_selective_programmes.concept: Real and common — many Canadian universities require applicants to apply directly to a specific faculty or program at the point of application (rather than a general 'university' application later streamed into a major), each with its own admission average, prerequisites, and sometimes its own supplementary application.
restricted_selective_programmes.faculty_specific_application_note: Examples: University of Waterloo Engineering is direct-entry per specific engineering program from day one, with its own Admission Information Form (AIF) and, per some programs, online interview submissions, in addition to the five-course academic prerequisite set; University of Toronto Engineering requires a supplementary personal-profile-style application covering extracurriculars, competitions, and work experience; Western University's Ivey Business School uses a distinct 'Advanced Entry Opportunity' (AEO) conditional pathway entered from high school but formally admitted in year three, with reported acceptance rates far tighter than general admission.
restricted_selective_programmes.explanation: This 'separate faculty/programme application' model means eligibility and competitiveness must be assessed at the programme level, not just the university level — the same applicant can be a strong candidate for one faculty at a university and a weak one for a different faculty at the identical institution.

admissions_decision_model.dominant_model: Predominantly a grades-threshold / admission-average model rather than the US-style broad holistic model — Canadian universities commonly publish (or effectively operate) a minimum and a separate, higher 'competitive' admission average for a given program/faculty, and the great majority of applicants are evaluated primarily against that average plus completed prerequisites.
admissions_decision_model.explanation: Admission averages are program-specific, not just university-specific (e.g., McGill's most competitive Engineering streams require averages around 95%+, while other programs at the same university require substantially less), and the actual average of admitted students often runs well above the published minimum at oversubscribed programs. Holistic, non-grade factors (supplementary personal-profile essays, portfolios, auditions, extracurricular evidence) genuinely do apply, but selectively — concentrated at specific universities (UBC) or specific competitive/creative/professional programmes (Music, Fine Art, Ivey AEO, some Engineering supplementary applications) rather than as a system-wide layer applied uniformly the way the US Common App essay is. No fake percentage weightings are asserted here; where a university describes a holistic process it is described qualitatively (e.g., 'considers grades, mandatory AIF responses, and interview submissions') without a disclosed numeric formula.

safe_inferences: Canada has no single national undergraduate application platform — this parallels the US finding and is well supported: OUAC, EducationPlannerBC, and ApplyAlberta are each strictly provincial in scope, and several provinces have no centralized platform at all.
Grades/transcript and completed subject prerequisites are the dominant admission signal across virtually all Canadian universities, more uniformly than in the US holistic model.
SAT/ACT are not a general requirement in Canada — a genuine, sourced system-level difference from the US.

IB predicted grades are operationally used by Canadian universities for conditional offers, confirmed against final results by a stated summer deadline — this is real and documented at multiple institutions (McGill, Alberta, Carleton), even though Canada lacks a UK-style universal conditional-offer mechanic tied to a single national platform.

Quebec is structurally distinct from the rest of Canada due to the mandatory CEGEP pre-university stage and the R-score evaluation system for CEGEP-origin applicants — this is not optional context, it materially changes the evaluation mechanism for anyone applying to a Quebec university as a CEGEP-track applicant.
No binding early-decision-style commitment mechanism was found operating anywhere in the Canadian system in the sources reviewed.
unsafe_inferences: Assuming 'Canada' has one uniform national admissions system or timeline — false; the system is provincial/university-specific with only three provinces (Ontario, BC, Alberta) having any centralized platform at all.
Assuming OUAC's Ontario-specific deadlines, fee structure, or application codes (101/105) apply nationally — they apply only to Ontario's OUAC-member universities.

Assuming a Turkish MEB diploma's exact numeric equivalency (e.g., 'MEB average X equals Canadian average Y') without checking each specific target university's own published country-requirement table — no Canada-wide equivalency table exists.

Assuming extracurriculars or personal essays are either universally required or universally absent in Canada — both UBC (heavy weight) and University of Toronto general admission (no essay, no extracurricular review) are real, opposite examples within the same country.

Assuming WES is a mandatory or standard step for undergraduate admission the way it more commonly is for Canadian immigration/professional licensing purposes — most large universities evaluate international secondary transcripts in-house.

Assuming a published 'minimum' admission average is sufficient for actual admission at competitive programs — the effectively-required (competitive) average is often 8-12+ percentage points above the published floor at oversubscribed programs.

eligibility_competitiveness_fit.eligibility: Whether a Turkish (or other international) applicant meets the specific target university's and target programme's published minimum credential/grade/subject-prerequisite bar — this must be checked per-university and per-programme, since there is no national or even reliably provincial eligibility standard in Canada.
eligibility_competitiveness_fit.competitiveness: Whether the applicant's actual academic average, subject grades, and (where applicable) supplementary evidence (personal profile, portfolio, audition, extracurricular depth) meet or exceed the realistic admitted-student range for that specific programme, which is commonly well above the published minimum at oversubscribed faculties (e.g., Engineering, Computer Science, Business at top-ranked universities).
eligibility_competitiveness_fit.fit: Whether the applicant's demonstrated interests, subject strengths, and (where the programme evaluates it) personal-profile narrative align with what that specific programme is designed to select for — most consequential at UBC-style holistic-profile institutions and at highly specialized/creative programmes (Music, Fine Art, direct-entry Engineering streams), less consequential at general Arts & Science admission driven purely by transcript average.

counselor_actions: First identify which province(s) the student's target universities are in, since application platform, deadline structure, and process differ meaningfully by province (Ontario/OUAC vs BC/EducationPlannerBC vs Alberta/ApplyAlberta vs direct-application provinces vs Quebec's CEGEP-linked system).

If applying to Ontario universities, use OUAC (101 for current Ontario high school students, 105 for international/out-of-province/mature applicants) and track the equal-consideration deadline (commonly mid-January) separately from each university's own supplementary/program-specific deadlines.
If applying to BC or Alberta public institutions, check whether EducationPlannerBC or ApplyAlberta covers the target school before assuming a direct application is required.

If applying to a Quebec university as a non-CEGEP (international) applicant, confirm the university evaluates international transcripts directly rather than through the R-score CEGEP pathway, which applies specifically to Quebec CEGEP graduates.

Verify each target university's published country-specific equivalency requirement for a Turkish MEB diploma directly on that university's own international admissions page — do not assume a uniform Canada-wide MEB threshold exists.

Confirm subject-prerequisite requirements (e.g., Calculus, Physics, Chemistry) for the specific target faculty/programme, since missing a prerequisite can disqualify an otherwise strong applicant regardless of overall average.

Check whether the target programme requires a separate faculty-specific application, supplementary personal-profile essay, portfolio, or audition beyond the general university application (common at UBC generally, and at Engineering/Music/Fine Art/Business programmes specifically at many universities).

For IB or A-Level students, plan for a conditional-offer workflow: predicted grades typically drive the initial offer, and final results must be submitted by a stated summer deadline (commonly around August) to confirm admission — build this into the student's application timeline and stress-test whether their predicted grades meet the specific programme's stated minimum.

Do not assume SAT/ACT is required — check the specific target university's policy before recommending the student invest time in standardized testing for Canada specifically, distinct from any US-bound testing plan the student may separately need.

data_model_implications.notes: Canada requires at minimum a province-aware layer between country and university (unlike a flatter US state-is-mostly-irrelevant-to-admission-process model, since in Canada the province genuinely determines which application platform, if any, applies). A conceptual 'application_platform' entity distinct from 'university' is needed, since one platform (OUAC, EducationPlannerBC, ApplyAlberta) maps to many universities within a single province, and most Canadian universities map to no platform at all (direct application). Quebec CEGEP-origin applicants need a distinct evaluation-mechanism flag (R-score) that does not apply to any other Canadian applicant type, analogous to how MEB/IB/A-Level are already distinct credential types in the existing ORYN model — R-score is not a credential type per se but a province-specific evaluation output derived from the CEGEP DEC credential.
gaps: Exact current-cycle OUAC fee schedule and definitive list of all OUAC application codes (106, 108, 109 exist per third-party sources but could not be confirmed from OUAC's own site, which returned 403 to automated fetches in this research pass).
Turkey-specific numeric grade/average thresholds at major Canadian universities (U of T's country-requirement page could not be paginated to the Turkey entry via automated fetch).
Confirmation of whether a Canada-specific foundation-year pathway exists at meaningful scale for underqualified Turkish/MEB applicants.
Deeper French Bac and German Abitur-specific equivalency data at named Canadian universities (out of scope depth for this pass; flagged for a follow-up research task if needed).

system_university_programme_override_mod.explanation: Canada has almost nothing that is genuinely national in undergraduate admissions — no national platform, no national deadline, no national credential-equivalency table, and no national admissions body. The next layer down, provincial, carries real and meaningful structure but only in specific provinces: Ontario has the most centralized structure via OUAC (shared platform, a common equal-consideration deadline, common application codes), Quebec has a structurally distinct system via the mandatory CEGEP stage and R-score mechanism (fundamentally changing how domestic Quebec-track applicants are evaluated versus everyone else), and BC/Alberta have meaningful but lighter-touch shared platforms (EducationPlannerBC, ApplyAlberta) that mostly simplify application logistics without imposing a uniform deadline or evaluation standard the way OUAC's equal-consideration deadline does. Below the provincial layer, the university layer carries most of the substantive admission policy (minimum averages, country-equivalency tables, language-test acceptance, essay/personal-profile requirements), and below that, the programme/faculty layer carries prerequisite courses, competitive averages, and supplementary application components (auditions, portfolios, AIFs). In short: almost nothing is national, a real but geographically limited provincial layer exists (strongest in Ontario and structurally distinct in Quebec), and the university/programme layers do the majority of the substantive admissions work — similar in spirit to the US 'almost nothing is national' finding, but with a genuine provincial layer in specific provinces that the US analysis did not find at the state level.

matrix_row.main_application_architecture: Decentralized nationally; province-specific centralization in Ontario (OUAC), BC (EducationPlannerBC), Alberta (ApplyAlberta); direct-to-university elsewhere; Quebec has a distinct CEGEP-linked pathway
matrix_row.central_platform: OUAC (Ontario only); EducationPlannerBC (BC only); ApplyAlberta (Alberta only); none nationally
matrix_row.direct_applications_possible: Yes — the default outside Ontario/BC/Alberta, and even within those provinces some institutions (e.g., RMC in Ontario) require direct application
matrix_row.application_choice_limits: No national cap; platform-specific base-fee-covered choice counts with extra per-choice fees beyond that (e.g., OUAC 105 reportedly covers up to 3 choices before added fees per third-party sources); no exclusivity or single-choice rule anywhere
matrix_row.predicted_grades_role: Used operationally for IB (and by pattern A-Level) applicants to support a conditional offer, confirmed against final results by a stated summer deadline; not a defining universal mechanic for domestic provincial-curriculum applicants
matrix_row.subject_prerequisites: Common and consequential at the programme level for Engineering, CS, Business, health-science-track programmes (e.g., Calculus, Physics, Chemistry with stated minimum grades)
matrix_row.standardized_tests: Generally not required; grades-and-transcript-based admission is the norm; SAT/ACT occasionally considered as supplementary evidence for some international applicants
matrix_row.language_proof: IELTS/TOEFL/PTE/Duolingo widely accepted; Canada-specific CAEL test also accepted at 180+ institutions and recognized by IRCC for the Student Direct Stream; exemptions common for applicants schooled substantially in English/French
matrix_row.essays_motivation: University-specific, not universal — ranges from none (U of T general Arts & Science) to a heavily weighted multi-question Personal Profile (UBC, required of nearly all high-school applicants)
matrix_row.recommendations: Generally not required for undergraduate admission at most institutions; exception rather than rule
matrix_row.extracurricular_role: Genuinely institution-dependent — ignored at some universities' general admission (U of T), heavily weighted at others (UBC); depth valued over breadth where considered at all
matrix_row.conditional_offers: Real and commonly used mechanism for students still completing secondary school, especially IB/A-Level applicants basing offers on predicted grades pending final results by a stated deadline
matrix_row.restricted_programmes: Common — many competitive faculties (Engineering, Business, Music, Fine Art) require a separate direct application with their own admission average, prerequisites, and sometimes supplementary components (AIF, interview, portfolio, audition)
matrix_row.turkiye_meb_direct_entry_complexity: Likely feasible for many programmes but not independently confirmed with specific numeric thresholds in this research pass; university-specific equivalency verification required per target school; AP/IB/A-Level held alongside MEB materially strengthens both eligibility clarity and competitiveness
matrix_row.dominant_counselor_risk: Treating Canada as a single system and transferring a UK-style (OUAC=UCAS) or US-style (Common-App-essay-centric) mental model wholesale, when in fact provincial and even individual-university variation is the operative reality, and the correct process (platform vs direct, essay-required vs not, predicted-grades-relevant vs not) depends entirely on which specific province and university the student is targeting

unresolved_questions: Exact current OUAC fee schedule and full list/definition of all active OUAC application codes beyond 101/105 (106, 108, 109 referenced by third-party sources, not confirmed from OUAC's own site due to automated-fetch blocking).

Turkey-specific numeric grade/average equivalency thresholds at major Canadian universities (e.g., University of Toronto's country-requirement page listing for Turkey specifically) — page structure prevented automated retrieval of the Turkey row in this pass.
Whether a foundation-year pathway is meaningfully used in Canada for underqualified Turkish/MEB applicants, and if so, at what scale/institutions.
French Bac and German Abitur-specific equivalency tables at named Canadian universities — not independently verified in this pass (flagged as a gap, not asserted).
